theory.intro: The **first-derivative test** classifies a stationary point from the sign of $f'(x)$ just left and just right of it. Positive then negative is a local maximum, negative then positive a local minimum. No sign change is a horizontal point of inflection.
facts: The nature of a stationary point is decided by the sign of $f'$ on each side, not by $f'$ at the point.
$f'$ changing from positive to negative across the point gives a **local maximum**, where the curve rises then falls.
$f'$ changing from negative to positive gives a **local minimum**, where the curve falls then rises.
The same sign of $f'$ on both sides gives a **horizontal point of inflection**, where the curve flattens without turning.
Choose test values close enough that no other stationary point lies between them and the point being classified.
A **slope table** lists $x$, the value of $f'(x)$ and a slope stroke $/$, $-$ or $\backslash$ for each test value.
steps: Choose a test value on each side of every stationary point
Record the sign of $f'(x)$ at each test value in a slope table
Read the sign pattern to classify each stationary point

workedExamples.question_text:
A function has its only stationary point between $-1$ and $1$ at $x=0$. Use the slope table to classify it.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&-1&0&1\\\hline f'(x)&6&0&-3\end{array}$
workedExamples.solution_text: The derivative is positive to the left and negative to the right of $x=0$. The curve rises then falls, so $x=0$ is a local maximum.

workedExamples.question_text: The derivative of a function is $f'(x)=2(x+1)(x-2)^2$. Find the stationary $x$-values and classify each using a slope table.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}2(x+1)(x-2)^2&=0\\x&=-1,\ 2\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}x&-2&-1&0&2&3\\\hline f'(x)&-32&0&8&0&8\\\text{Slope}&\backslash&-&/&-&/\end{array}$

At $x=-1$, $f'$ changes from negative to positive: a local minimum.

At $x=2$, $f'$ is positive on both sides: a horizontal point of inflection.

workedExamples.question_text: Find the stationary points of $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1$ and determine their nature using a slope table.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3x^2-12x+9\\&=3(x-1)(x-3)\end{aligned}$

For stationary points:
$\begin{aligned}3(x-1)(x-3)&=0\\x&=1,\ 3\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}x&0&1&2&3&4\\\hline f'(x)&9&0&-3&0&9\\\text{Slope}&/&-&\backslash&-&/\end{array}$

$\begin{aligned}f(1)&=1-6+9+1=5\\f(3)&=27-54+27+1=1\end{aligned}$

The sign changes from positive to negative at $x=1$, giving a local maximum at $(1,5)$.

The sign changes from negative to positive at $x=3$, giving a local minimum at $(3,1)$.

workedExamples.question_text: Find and classify the stationary point of $f(x)=xe^{-3x}$ using the first-derivative test.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=e^{-3x}-3xe^{-3x}\\&=e^{-3x}(1-3x)\end{aligned}$

Since $e^{-3x}>0$, solve:
$\begin{aligned}1-3x&=0\\x&=\frac13\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&0&\frac13&1\\\hline f'(x)&1&0&-2e^{-3}\\\text{Slope}&/&-&\backslash\end{array}$

$\begin{aligned}f\left(\frac13\right)&=\frac13e^{-1}\\&=\frac{1}{3e}\end{aligned}$

The derivative changes from positive to negative, so $\left(\frac13,\frac{1}{3e}\right)$ is a local maximum.

workedExamples.question_text: Find and classify all stationary points of $f(x)=x^2e^{-2x}$ using the first-derivative test.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=2xe^{-2x}-2x^2e^{-2x}\\&=2xe^{-2x}(1-x)\end{aligned}$

Since $e^{-2x}>0$, the stationary points occur when:
$\begin{aligned}2x(1-x)&=0\\x&=0,\ 1\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}x&-1&0&\frac12&1&2\\\hline f'(x)&-4e^2&0&\frac{1}{2e}&0&-4e^{-4}\\\text{Slope}&\backslash&-&/&-&\backslash\end{array}$

$f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=e^{-2}$.

At $x=0$, the sign changes from negative to positive: a local minimum at $(0,0)$.

At $x=1$, the sign changes from positive to negative: a local maximum at $(1,e^{-2})$.

workedExamples.question_text:
For each function, find and classify its stationary point using the first-derivative test.

a. $f(x)=3\ln x-x$, $x>0$.

b. $g(x)=x^2\ln(2x)$, $x>0$.

c. $h(x)=\dfrac{\ln(2x)}{x}$, $x>0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
a. $f'(x)=\dfrac3x-1$.

$\begin{aligned}\frac3x-1&=0\\x&=3\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&1&3&6\\\hline f'(x)&2&0&-\frac12\\\text{Slope}&/&-&\backslash\end{array}$

The derivative changes from positive to negative. The local maximum is $(3,3\ln3-3)$.

b. Use the product and chain rules:
$\begin{aligned}g'(x)&=2x\ln(2x)+x^2\frac1x\\&=x\bigl(2\ln(2x)+1\bigr)\end{aligned}$

Since $x>0$:
$\begin{aligned}2\ln(2x)+1&=0\\\ln(2x)&=-\frac12\\x&=\frac{1}{2\sqrt e}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&\frac{1}{2e}&\frac{1}{2\sqrt e}&\frac12\\\hline g'(x)&-\frac{1}{2e}&0&\frac12\\\text{Slope}&\backslash&-&/\end{array}$

$g\left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt e}\right)=\dfrac{1}{4e}\left(-\dfrac12\right)=-\dfrac{1}{8e}$.

The derivative changes from negative to positive. The local minimum is $\left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt e},-\dfrac{1}{8e}\right)$.

c. Use the quotient rule:
$\begin{aligned}h'(x)&=\frac{x\left(\frac1x\right)-\ln(2x)}{x^2}\\&=\frac{1-\ln(2x)}{x^2}\end{aligned}$

Since $x^2>0$:
$\begin{aligned}1-\ln(2x)&=0\\\ln(2x)&=1\\x&=\frac e2\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&\frac12&\frac e2&\frac{e^2}{2}\\\hline h'(x)&4&0&-4e^{-4}\\\text{Slope}&/&-&\backslash\end{array}$

$h\left(\dfrac e2\right)=\dfrac{1}{e/2}=\dfrac2e$.

The derivative changes from positive to negative. The local maximum is $\left(\dfrac e2,\dfrac2e\right)$.

workedExamples.question_text: Find and classify the stationary points of $f(x)=2\sin x-x$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$, using the first-derivative test.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$f'(x)=2\cos x-1$.

For stationary points:
$\begin{aligned}2\cos x-1&=0\\\cos x&=\frac12\\x&=\frac\pi3,\ \frac{5\pi}3\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}x&0&\frac\pi3&\pi&\frac{5\pi}3&2\pi\\\hline f'(x)&1&0&-3&0&1\\\text{Slope}&/&-&\backslash&-&/\end{array}$

$\begin{aligned}f\left(\frac\pi3\right)&=\sqrt3-\frac\pi3\\f\left(\frac{5\pi}3\right)&=-\sqrt3-\frac{5\pi}3\end{aligned}$

At $x=\dfrac\pi3$, the sign changes from positive to negative: a local maximum at $\left(\dfrac\pi3,\sqrt3-\dfrac\pi3\right)$.

At $x=\dfrac{5\pi}3$, the sign changes from negative to positive: a local minimum at $\left(\dfrac{5\pi}3,-\sqrt3-\dfrac{5\pi}3\right)$.

workedExamples.question_text: Find and classify the stationary points of $f(x)=2x+2\sin x$ for $-2\pi<x<2\pi$, using the first-derivative test.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$f'(x)=2+2\cos x$.

$\begin{aligned}2+2\cos x&=0\\\cos x&=-1\\x&=-\pi,\ \pi\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}x&-\frac{3\pi}2&-\pi&0&\pi&\frac{3\pi}2\\\hline f'(x)&2&0&4&0&2\\\text{Slope}&/&-&/&-&/\end{array}$

Since $1+\cos x>0$ immediately on both sides of each stationary point, the derivative stays positive across both points.

$f(-\pi)=-2\pi$ and $f(\pi)=2\pi$.

Both $(-\pi,-2\pi)$ and $(\pi,2\pi)$ are horizontal points of inflection.

workedExamples.question_text: Find and classify the stationary points of $f(x)=x\sqrt{25-x^2}$ using a slope table. Give their coordinates exactly.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The domain is $-5\le x\le5$. Differentiate for $-5<x<5$:
$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\sqrt{25-x^2}+x\frac{-2x}{2\sqrt{25-x^2}}\\&=\frac{25-2x^2}{\sqrt{25-x^2}}\end{aligned}$

The denominator is positive in this interval, so stationary points satisfy:
$\begin{aligned}25-2x^2&=0\\x^2&=\frac{25}{2}\\x&=\pm\frac5{\sqrt2}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}x&-4&-\frac5{\sqrt2}&0&\frac5{\sqrt2}&4\\\hline f'(x)&-\frac73&0&5&0&-\frac73\\\text{Slope}&\backslash&-&/&-&\backslash\end{array}$

$\begin{aligned}f\left(-\frac5{\sqrt2}\right)&=-\frac5{\sqrt2}\frac5{\sqrt2}=-\frac{25}{2}\\f\left(\frac5{\sqrt2}\right)&=\frac5{\sqrt2}\frac5{\sqrt2}=\frac{25}{2}\end{aligned}$

At $x=-\dfrac5{\sqrt2}$, the derivative changes from negative to positive: a local minimum at $\left(-\dfrac5{\sqrt2},-\dfrac{25}{2}\right)$.

At $x=\dfrac5{\sqrt2}$, the derivative changes from positive to negative: a local maximum at $\left(\dfrac5{\sqrt2},\dfrac{25}{2}\right)$.

foundation.question_text:
A curve $y = f(x)$ has its only stationary point between $3$ and $5$ at $x = 4$, and these values of the derivative are known.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline f'(x) & -7 & 0 & 6 \end{array}$
Classify the stationary point.
foundation.solution_text:
$f'(3) = -7 < 0$, so the curve is falling to the left of $x = 4$.
$f'(5) = 6 > 0$, so the curve is rising to the right of $x = 4$.
The sign of $f'$ changes from negative to positive, so $x = 4$ is a local minimum.

foundation.question_text:
A curve $y = f(x)$ has its only stationary point at $x = 2$, and these values of the derivative are known.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline f'(x) & 5 & 0 & 8 \end{array}$
Classify the stationary point.
foundation.solution_text:
$f'(1) = 5 > 0$ and $f'(3) = 8 > 0$, so the curve is rising on both sides.
The sign of $f'$ does not change, so $x = 2$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

foundation.question_text:
The derivative of $y = f(x)$ is $f'(x) = (x - 2)(x + 5)$.
Classify the stationary point at $x = -5$.
foundation.solution_text:
$f'(-6) = (-8)(-1) = 8 > 0$
$f'(-4) = (-6)(1) = -6 < 0$
The sign of $f'$ changes from positive to negative, so $x = -5$ is a local maximum.

foundation.question_text:
The derivative of $y = f(x)$ is $f'(x) = -3(x - 1)(x - 7)$.
Classify the stationary point at $x = 1$.
foundation.solution_text:
$f'(0) = -3(-1)(-7) = -21 < 0$
$f'(2) = -3(1)(-5) = 15 > 0$
The sign of $f'$ changes from negative to positive, so $x = 1$ is a local minimum.

foundation.question_text:
The derivative of $y = f(x)$ is $f'(x) = (x + 4)^2$.
Classify the stationary point at $x = -4$.
foundation.solution_text:
$f'(-5) = (-1)^2 = 1 > 0$
$f'(-3) = (1)^2 = 1 > 0$
A square is never negative, so $f'$ keeps the same sign on both sides.
There is no sign change, so $x = -4$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

foundation.question_text: Find the stationary point of $f(x) = xe^{x}$ and classify it using the first-derivative test.
foundation.solution_text:
1. **Differentiate to find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(x) = 0$**
$f'(x) = e^{x} + xe^{x}$
$= e^{x}(1 + x)$
Since $e^{x} > 0$ for all $x$, $f'(x) = 0$ when $1 + x = 0$.
$x = -1$
$f(-1) = -e^{-1}$
2. **Record the sign of $f'(x)$ at each test value in a slope table**
$f'(-2) = e^{-2}(-1) < 0$
$f'(0) = e^{0}(1) = 1 > 0$
The sign changes from negative to positive, so there is a local minimum at $\left(-1, -\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$.

             xtick={-3,-2,-1,1}, ytick={-1,1,2,3}]
\addplot[smooth, thick, <->, domain=-3.8:1.05] {x*exp(x)};
\addplot[only marks, mark=*] coordinates {(-1,-0.3679)};

foundation.question_text: Find the stationary point of $f(x) = \ln x - x$ for $x > 0$ and classify it using the first-derivative test.
foundation.solution_text:
$f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{x} - 1$
Set $f'(x) = 0$:
$\dfrac{1}{x} = 1$
$x = 1$
$f(1) = \ln 1 - 1 = -1$
$f'\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 - 1 = 1 > 0$
$f'(2) = \tfrac{1}{2} - 1 = -\tfrac{1}{2} < 0$
The sign changes from positive to negative, so there is a local maximum at $(1, -1)$.

foundation.question_text:
The curve $f(x) = \sin x + \cos x$ has a stationary point at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ in the domain $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
Classify it using the first-derivative test.
foundation.solution_text:
$f'(x) = \cos x - \sin x$
$f'(0) = 1 - 0 = 1 > 0$
$f'\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0 - 1 = -1 < 0$
The sign changes from positive to negative, so $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is a local maximum.
$f\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \sqrt{2}$
The local maximum is at $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \sqrt{2}\right)$.

development.question_text: Find and classify the stationary point of $f(x) = xe^{-2x}$.
development.solution_text:
$f'(x) = e^{-2x} - 2xe^{-2x}$
$= e^{-2x}(1 - 2x)$
Set $f'(x) = 0$. Since $e^{-2x} > 0$, $1 - 2x = 0$.
$x = \dfrac{1}{2}$
$f\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \tfrac{1}{2}e^{-1}$
$f'(0) = 1 > 0$
$f'(1) = e^{-2}(-1) < 0$
The sign changes from positive to negative, so there is a local maximum at $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2e}\right)$.

development.question_text: Find and classify the stationary point of $f(x) = (x - 3)e^{x}$.
development.solution_text:
$f'(x) = e^{x} + (x - 3)e^{x}$
$= e^{x}(x - 2)$
Set $f'(x) = 0$. Since $e^{x} > 0$, $x - 2 = 0$.
$x = 2$
$f(2) = -e^{2}$
$f'(1) = e(1 - 2) < 0$
$f'(3) = e^{3}(3 - 2) > 0$
The sign changes from negative to positive, so there is a local minimum at $\left(2, -e^{2}\right)$.

development.question_text: Find and classify the stationary point of $f(x) = x^{2}\ln x$ for $x > 0$.
development.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 2x\ln x + x$
$= x(2\ln x + 1)$
Set $f'(x) = 0$. Since $x > 0$, $2\ln x + 1 = 0$.
$\ln x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$
$x = e^{-\frac{1}{2}}$
$f'\left(e^{-2}\right) = e^{-2}(-4 + 1) < 0$
$f'(1) = 1(0 + 1) = 1 > 0$
The sign changes from negative to positive, so there is a local minimum.
$f\left(e^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) = e^{-1}\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2e}$
The local minimum is at $\left(e^{-\frac{1}{2}}, -\dfrac{1}{2e}\right)$.

development.question_text: Find and classify the stationary points of $f(x) = x + \sin x$ for $-2\pi < x < 2\pi$.
development.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 1 + \cos x$
Set $f'(x) = 0$:
$\cos x = -1$
$x = -\pi$ or $x = \pi$
Since $\cos x \ge -1$ for every $x$, $f'(x) = 1 + \cos x \ge 0$ everywhere.
The derivative is positive on both sides of each point, so neither is a turning point.
There are horizontal points of inflection at $(-\pi, -\pi)$ and $(\pi, \pi)$.

development.question_text: Find and classify the stationary points of $f(x) = 2\sin x + x$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
development.solution_text:
1. **Differentiate to find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(x) = 0$**
$f'(x) = 2\cos x + 1$
$\cos x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$
$x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ or $x = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$
2. **Record the sign of $f'(x)$ at each test value in a slope table**
$f'\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0 + 1 = 1 > 0$
$f'(\pi) = -2 + 1 = -1 < 0$
$f'\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 0 + 1 = 1 > 0$
At $x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ the sign changes from positive to negative, a local maximum at $\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \sqrt{3} + \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$.
At $x = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ the sign changes from negative to positive, a local minimum at $\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3}\right)$.

development.question_text:
The curve $f(x) = x\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}$ has derivative $f'(x) = \dfrac{9 - 2x^{2}}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}}$ for $-3 < x < 3$.
Classify the stationary point at $x = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$.
development.solution_text:
The denominator $\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}$ is positive throughout $-3 < x < 3$, so the sign of $f'$ is the sign of $9 - 2x^{2}$.
$f'(2) = \dfrac{9 - 8}{\sqrt{5}} > 0$
$f'(2.5) = \dfrac{9 - 12.5}{\sqrt{2.75}} < 0$
The sign changes from positive to negative, so there is a local maximum.
$f\left(\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \times \sqrt{9 - \tfrac{9}{2}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \times \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{9}{2}$
The local maximum is at $\left(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}, \dfrac{9}{2}\right)$.

development.question_text: Find the stationary points of $f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 9x + 2$ and determine their nature using the first-derivative test.
development.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 3x^{2} - 6x - 9 = 3(x + 1)(x - 3)$
Set $f'(x) = 0$:
$x = -1$ or $x = 3$
$f(-1) = -1 - 3 + 9 + 2 = 7$
$f(3) = 27 - 27 - 27 + 2 = -25$
$f'(-2) = 3(-1)(-5) = 15 > 0$
$f'(0) = 3(1)(-3) = -9 < 0$
$f'(4) = 3(5)(1) = 15 > 0$
At $x = -1$ the sign changes from positive to negative, so there is a local maximum at $(-1, 7)$.
At $x = 3$ the sign changes from negative to positive, so there is a local minimum at $(3, -25)$.

development.question_text:
A curve $y = f(x)$ has stationary points only at $x = -1$ and $x = 2$, and these values of the derivative are known.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & -2 & -1 & 0 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline f'(x) & 8 & 0 & -4 & 0 & 9 \end{array}$
Classify both stationary points.
development.solution_text:
Across $x = -1$ the sign of $f'$ goes from $+8$ to $-4$, a change from positive to negative.
So $x = -1$ is a local maximum.
Across $x = 2$ the sign of $f'$ goes from $-4$ to $+9$, a change from negative to positive.
So $x = 2$ is a local minimum.

mastery.question_text: Find and classify all stationary points of $f(x) = x^{2}e^{-x}$.
mastery.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 2xe^{-x} - x^{2}e^{-x}$
$= xe^{-x}(2 - x)$
Since $e^{-x} > 0$, $f'(x) = 0$ when $x = 0$ or $x = 2$.
$f(0) = 0$ and $f(2) = 4e^{-2}$
$f'(-1) = (-1)e^{1}(3) < 0$
$f'(1) = (1)e^{-1}(1) > 0$
$f'(3) = (3)e^{-3}(-1) < 0$
At $x = 0$ the sign changes from negative to positive, a local minimum at $(0, 0)$.
At $x = 2$ the sign changes from positive to negative, a local maximum at $\left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^{2}}\right)$.

mastery.question_text:
The derivative of $y = f(x)$ is $f'(x) = x^{2}(x - 4)^{3}$.
Classify every stationary point of $y = f(x)$.
mastery.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 0$ when $x = 0$ or $x = 4$.
$f'(-1) = (1)(-125) = -125 < 0$
$f'(1) = (1)(-27) = -27 < 0$
There is no sign change at $x = 0$, so it is a horizontal point of inflection.
$f'(3) = (9)(-1) = -9 < 0$
$f'(5) = (25)(1) = 25 > 0$
The sign changes from negative to positive at $x = 4$, so it is a local minimum.

mastery.question_text:
The derivative of $y = f(x)$ is $f'(x) = 4(x + 2)(x - 1)^{2}$.
Find the $x$-coordinates of every stationary point and use a table of gradients to classify them.
mastery.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 0$ when $x = -2$ or $x = 1$.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & -3 & -2 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline f'(x) & -64 & 0 & 8 & 0 & 16 \end{array}$
At $x = -2$ the sign changes from negative to positive, so it is a local minimum.
At $x = 1$ the derivative is positive on both sides, so there is a horizontal point of inflection.

mastery.question_text: Find and classify the stationary point of $f(x) = \dfrac{\ln x}{x}$ for $x > 0$.
mastery.solution_text:
$f'(x) = \dfrac{x \times \frac{1}{x} - \ln x \times 1}{x^{2}}$
$= \dfrac{1 - \ln x}{x^{2}}$
Set $f'(x) = 0$. Since $x^{2} > 0$, $1 - \ln x = 0$.
$\ln x = 1$
$x = e$
$f'(1) = \dfrac{1 - 0}{1} = 1 > 0$
$f'\left(e^{2}\right) = \dfrac{1 - 2}{e^{4}} < 0$
The sign changes from positive to negative, so there is a local maximum at $\left(e, \dfrac{1}{e}\right)$.
